en: Preface to the *Luohu Yalu*:
Out of weariness with travel, I returned to rest upon the banks of the Luohu River. Shuttering my door and sweeping away visitors, I withdrew from the world.
Consequently, I reflected back upon my past wanderings through the monastic forests; the sayings and deeds of former sages that I have heard and witnessed are not few. Perhaps...

I have obtained [teachings] from the exhortations of venerable seniors and the discourses of my friends; or I have found them in broken steles, fragmentary tablets, moth-eaten scrolls, and ancient volumes.

As the years and months have long passed, I fear they might fall into oblivion. Therefore, I have not further sorted or rearranged them, but have instead compiled them into a single collection according to their chronological order of acquisition, titling it *The Wild Record of Lake Luo*.
However, as the times differ and circumstances vary, I truly fear that [these teachings] may be transmitted...

I have heard that these errors and contradictions would merely serve to defile the legacy of the former masters and invite derision from future generations. For now, I shall privately preserve this work to await a critical revision.
Should a learned scholar arise who wields the pen of Dong Hu to compose a "History of the Jewel of the Sangha" (*Sengbao Shi*), they may take this and supplement it;
thus, its crude fragments and omissions will not be without benefit.
Preface by the Buddhist disciple (Xiao Ying) of Huye Hall on the full moon day of the tenth month in the Yihai year of the Xiangxing era.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xiao Ying of Jiangxi during the Song Dynasty. *Luohu Yalu*, Volume One.
During his ordinary life, Zhao Qingxian took Chan Master Yuan of Tianbo in Bei Jing as his friend beyond the secular world and consulted him regarding the Dharma of the mind.

Later, while serving as the governor of Qingzhou, he heard a clap of thunder daily and attained a realization. He immediately spoke this verse: "Retiring from my meal at the official hall, I lean against the desk;
Unmoving and unshaken, my mind is like water. A single peal of thunder penetrates the gate of the crown; It startles me awake from my sleep."
Regarding that which is fundamentally within oneself: "Lifting one's head, the azure sky—joy upon joy! In every land and in every atom of dust, there is nothing that is not so.

Those of inferior or middling capacity cannot hear this; it is merely the wondrous functioning of spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*). Thereafter, he replied in a letter to the Duke of Zheng (Fu Yi), stating briefly:

"Recently, I dispatched a courier with three volumes of the *Jie-ben Chuan-deng* (The Source Text of the Transmission of the Lamp). You must have already received them. Now, I have received your decree regarding Song Wei..."

Setting aside the remaining seven scrolls for later inclusion, I prostrate with joy and contemplate that the Dharma of the Western Sage’s "separate transmission outside the teachings" was not established for those of middling or inferior faculties.
Those of superior wisdom enter through sudden enlightenment; once attained, it is attained forever.

The ignorant, however, remain deluded and do not return to the truth; thus there arise a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions. Only the Buddhas and Patriarchs have transmitted mind-to-mind.

When they were compelled to benefit sentient beings and gather in all things, they consequently employed various expedient means: blows with staffs and shouts, punches and pointing with fingers, raising eyebrows and blinking eyes, striking the mallet and holding up the whisk, as well as speech, words, and written characters.
As the distance from the Sages grew ever greater, the disciples of various quarters forgot [the true essence].
This is to pursue the branches while neglecting the root, to abandon the source while following the waves; such rampant flames are all pervasive—this is truly what is called "pitiable.

Your humble servant, Bei, was in Qingzhou at the beginning of last autumn. Having been moved by certain realizations, I have come to know somewhat that one's original nature is neither deficient nor redundant.
As the ancients called it the "Dharma-gate of Peace and Bliss," I believe this is no false claim. Recently, I have received the grace of the Grand Tutor and Palace Attendant...

I have sought out the records of Chan literature. Having long been favored by your grace and benevolence, upon hearing this, I was filled with joy and delight; I could not help but dance with my hands and tread with my feet.

I humbly observe that your Excellency’s wealth and honor are at such an ultimate height, your virtue and morality are so flourishing, your blessings, longevity, health, and tranquility are so fully endowed, and your retirement and leisure are so sublime.
Yet, there is one thing upon which you have not yet bestowed much attention: [the study of Chan].

This is nothing other than the Tathāgata’s single great causal event (*ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu*). Now, having again attained realization and entry into true nature (*tathatā*), I venture to offer my congratulations to your honor.
You have expressed what you have realized upon this sheet of silk, serving as a fellow practitioner alongside Zheng Gong;
this is surely because you have not failed the entrustment of the former Sage. During the Yuanfeng era, [you served] as the Junior Master of the Heir Apparent...

Ba returned to Sanqu. Among the local villagers, he made no distinction between their status or appearance. He named his residence "Gaozhai" (The High Studio) and composed a verse to express its meaning, which says:
"Girded with gold, I have already retired and hidden away; The message within this is simply ordinary.

If people of the age wish to know the old man of Gaozhai, He is none other than Zhao Sili of Ke Village. Furthermore, he recorded the inscription for his burial site, saying: "My official duties have been brought to completion."
His lifespan was seventy-two years. After his hundredth year, he returned to this mountain site. That true Dharma-body is neither identical to nor separate from it;
it fills the great trichiliocosm, universally manifesting compassion and wisdom. It cannot be hidden away, nor can it be placed anywhere. Such is the account of his life-span and burial mound.
So it is. So it is. Observing the leakage of his family tradition, there is not a single word left unsaid. How could one allow Pei and Pang to monopolize such beauty in the past?

As for one who withdraws from the world yet achieves renown, who maintains excellence from beginning to end, who does not step beyond the threshold of his courtyard, whose mind accords with that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—this is far superior to those who know how to avoid calamity by seizing the opportune moment, and who speak of departing to roam with Master Chisongzi; the latter are worlds apart.
Chan Master Jingduan of Xiyu in Huzhou, whose courtesy name was Piaoming, was born into the Qiu family of Guian in Huzhou.

At the age of six, he entered the service of Baoyuan at Jiekong Monastery on Mount Wu as his teacher. Several times, Baoyuan wished to enroll him using funds for the state registry (*jinna seng*), but Jingduan declined, saying, "My aspiration is not to become a registered monk through payment;
it would not be too late for me to devote myself to study and count among the ranks of those who serve the Triple Gem. He was [sixteen] years old.
At twenty-six, he first obtained the monastic robes. Shortly thereafter, while watching and playing with lions, he suddenly attained realization of the Dharma of the mind.

He then followed Master Renyue to receive the essential principles of the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*. One day, Renyue presented ten or so difficult points from the sutra and tasked his disciples with answering them;
only Zhiyan presented two verses, saying: "The heart was sought in seven locations, yet the heart was not found; Dazed and bewildered, O..."
"It is difficult not to have a sudden flash of insight. Even if you were to investigate until you see the state of no-mind, it would still be like washing a clod of earth in the mud.
He further said, "The teaching of the 'eight returns' has been handed down for a long time; since antiquity, the patriarchal masters have each analyzed it.

Even if you could reach the moment when there is neither returning nor non-returning, it would still be like a shrimp leaping but unable to escape the bucket. Yue looked at him with astonishment and said, "Your realization and vision are lofty and subtle; you must surely..."
At that time, Chan Master Qiyue resided at Longhua in Hangzhou, and his reputation for the Way shone brightly throughout Eastern Wu.
Xuedou went there to pay his respects; their spiritual affinity was so well-matched that, without realizing it, Xuedou suddenly leaped up and turned over like a lion cub.

Qiyue therefore approved of him, and from then on, the monastic community respectfully called him "Xuedou the Lion. Xuedou was naturally compassionate and kind, and he was scrupulous in observing the precepts.

[This is] contrary [to principle]. To show compassion for the hungry and inquire after the cold as if it were one's own urgent concern—when Chancellor Zhang Zhitou returned to Wu from the Central Secretariat, he brought Chengdu to reside at Mount Ling.
Later, when an imperial decree arrived appointing him to office, Chengdu’s father happened to be unwell;

thus, he was unable to decide whether to proceed or withdraw. Chengdu offered him this verse: "It is easy to turn iron into gold, But difficult to fulfill both loyalty and filial piety. Consider this carefully."
[The Master] remarked: "It is not as leisurely as that of an idle wild monk like me, beneath the ancient pine tree at Lingshan Guxiao Chan Monastery in Changxing, Huzhou.
He also once traveled to Jinling to visit Lord Wang Jinggong, as the latter was in office reforming the various affairs of state.

Thus he composed a verse: *Namo Avalokiteśvara.* *He expounds various teachings,* *Yet the ocean of sentient beings' karma is deep;* *Therefore, they are difficult to rescue.* *Those who frequently sink and drown* *Utter cries of resentment against the Bodhisattva.* Liu Tao of Wuxing composed this inscription for the Endu Pagoda.
Whenever Jingzhou saw the verses spoken by Endu, he would praise them, saying: "Because he possesses the fundamental source, it is thus."
However, the two verses offered to the two gentlemen both emerged from the playful exercise of dhyāna-joy.
Had they not encountered one who possesses the Way beyond the mundane, they would surely have incurred reproach and censure. Can this not be called "forgetting each other within the Daoist arts"?
The nun Kōngshì was the daughter of Fan Gong Xun, who served as a Director of the Dragon Diagram Pavilion. From her youth, she was intelligent and took delight in meditative stillness.
Consequently, while her elder brother was serving as an official in Fēnníng, Yúzhāng, she went to visit Chanshi Sīxīn at Yúnyán.
Having grasped the essential meaning beneath these words, he immediately offered praise to Sīxin in verse, saying: "Sīxin of Shaoyang, the source of spirit is profoundly deep.
In the ears one sees forms; within the eyes one hears sounds. Ordinary men are enlightened while sages are obscured; The later is wealthy while the earlier is poor.
Benefiting beings and aiding all things, you turn iron into gold. Though brush and ink might labor to depict it, it is neither ancient nor modern. Sīxin asked him, "Death?"
The mind is not real; toward what, then, can one offer praise? If one praises the "dead mind," the dead mind has no form.
If one praises empty space, empty space leaves no trace. Having neither form nor trace, what words can be uttered?

If one can utter such words, one will have personally seen the dead mind. He replied: "The dead mind is not real; reality is not the dead mind. Empty space is formless; wondrous existence is shapeless."
Having been brought to a dead end, he revived once more and personally encountered Sīti-mati (Sīxin). Thereupon, Sīti-mati merely smiled.

Master Lingyuan subsequently bestowed upon him the title "Wayman of the Empty Chamber" (Kōngshì dàorén). From that time on, he became renowned throughout the monastic communities. During the Zhenghe era, he resided in Jinling.
At that time, Chan Master Yuǎnwù was staying at Jiāngshān, and Chan Master Foyǎn was also there. Because their words and spiritual resonance accorded with one another, the two masters...

He praised him, yet Dao-yun’s demeanor was so tranquil and simple that he appeared as if unable to speak. When it came to elucidating right view, however, his elegant verses were refined and incisive.
There is one who read the *Fajie guan*: "Objects and self are fundamentally non-dual; the myriad phenomena are like reflections in a mirror."
Brilliantly transcending principal and attendant, clearly penetrating the true void; one essence containing manifold dharmas, interlacing within the Indra’s net.
With infinite layers of inexhaustible meaning, both movement and stillness are perfectly pervasive. Furthermore, he established a bath at Baoning and posted a notice at the gate that said:
"If there is not a single thing, what is there to wash? If there were even a speck of dust, from where would it arise? State one [word].
The sentences are profound; only then can the Great Master enter the bath. Guling only knew how to scrub backs; how could the Bodhisattva have ever clarified his mind?

When one wishes to realize the Ground of Freedom from Defilement, it is necessary for sweat to break out over the entire body. Everyone says that water can wash away defilements, but who knows that water itself is also dust?
Even if water and defilement are suddenly removed, when one reaches this point, even that must be washed away. Later, at Gufeng...
Su Xi-zhu entered the convent to shave her head and become a nun, taking the name Wei Jiu. In the sixth year of the Xuanhe era, she passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
Born into a noble lineage, Dao-ren was not ensnared by wealth or status; she stood out as one who followed in the footsteps of Candrottarā, heading directly toward unsurpassed Bodhi.
Furthermore, she changed her appearance and dress to associate with the lowly, such as the iron-grinder woman. Thus, at the moment of life and death, she acted as an example.
This is a testament to his extraordinary nature. Were it not for a will as fierce as autumn frost, who could have achieved such a thing?
During the Yuanyou era, Huang Gong Lüzhi, the Grand Historian, was observing mourning for his parents and was staying at Mount Huanglong, where he studied under Master Huìtáng.
He formed particularly deep bonds of spiritual friendship with the elders Sīxīn and Língyuán, both of whom were outside the conventional world. Consequently, Huìtáng...
In the course of conversation, he cited: "Confucius said to his disciples, 'Do you think I am concealing anything from you? I conceal nothing from you.
There is no action of mine that I do not share with you, my disciples; such is the person of Qiu. Thereupon, [the Master] requested that Gong explain this, doing so repeatedly.
Huìtáng did not approve of his interpretation. Gong’s anger manifested on his face, and after remaining silent for a long time, it happened that the summer heat had subsided.
A coolness arose; the autumn fragrance filled the courtyard. Huìtáng then asked, "Do you smell the scent of the *mùxī* (cassia)?
The Master replied, “I do. Huìtáng said, “I have revealed nothing hidden to you. The Master joyfully attained understanding. Later, while in Qiānnán, he sent a letter to Sīxīn, saying:
In the past, I was frequently exhorted by your bitter words, yet I remained as if in a drunken dream, lingering vaguely within the shadows of light.

This was because my doubts were not fully resolved and the root of my life-destiny was not severed; thus, I retreated, turning back from the precipice. I am currently on the way to Qinzhou, having been banished from office.
Upon waking from my midday sleep, I was suddenly struck by a vast, open clarity. I reflected on how, throughout my life, I had been deceived by the old monks of the world for so long;
only Master Sīnmind (Sīnmindàopǐn) refused to grant me his seal of approval, and that was precisely his greatest act of compassion for me.
Linyuan sent him a verse, saying: "In the past, facing each other, we were a thousand li apart; Now, ten thousand li away, we are even more intimate. In silent solitude..."
The flavor is the same as plain gruel; in joyful conversation, host and guest reach accord. Within the room, who is permitted to question the transforming woman?
Do not seek the pupil within your own eyes. East, west, south, and north—there is nowhere to hide; the golden-headed *dhūta* laughs ever more freshly.
Master He said: "The stonemason comes to chip away the dust from the tip of the nose; the handless man arrives and the axe becomes intimate. The white ox and the tabby cat—their minds are Buddha.
The dragon-eyed and tiger-eyed ones are guest within host. Carrying his own jar, he goes to buy village wine; putting on his robe, he returns to act as host.
Ten thousand miles apart, they always face one another; within Dead Heart’s quarters, there is freshness. Huang.
The Duke served as the leader of the literary community, yet he was able to apply his keen resolve to this Way. In Qian-nan, his spiritual resonance was met with profound response;

through his letters he revealed its essence, and through his verses he brought it to full expression. Thus, the harmonious accord between him and the two elders, Qing and Xin, can be clearly discerned. Alas!

That which is most highly esteemed in the world is the Way alone. Since you, sir, have thoroughly investigated and clarified it, how could Du Fu’s remark that "literature is but a minor art" be anything other than true?
Chan Master P’an-an Cheng was surnamed Liu by birth and was a native of Yichun. He discarded his Confucian robes and cap to don the *saṃghāṭī* at Mount Yang.
Subsequently, he received the supramundane Dharma from Master Ping, known as Puyong. At the beginning of the Xuande era (1119–1125), he resided at Jingyin Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
When Grand Marshal Chen Liangbi convened a great assembly, Chan and lecture masters gathered from all quarters; among them was the Dharma Master Shan of the Xianshou school.

The eminent master [Zongmi] sent inquiries to various Chan masters, saying: "Our Buddha established the teachings ranging from the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) up to the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*).

These teach that one must first eliminate both emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*bhāva*), and alone realize the True and Constant (*zhen-chang*). Only after being adorned with the myriad virtues can one be called a Buddha.

Yet, the Chan school claims that through a single shout (*he*), one transforms from an ordinary person into a sage. Examining the various sutras and treatises, this seems to be in contradiction. Now, if a single shout can indeed..."
To enter the Five Teachings is the correct exposition; if one cannot enter the Five Teachings, it is a false exposition.
At that time, the various Chan practitioners were seated in rows. Chan Master Fazhen (Master Yi) signaled with his eyes to Chan Master Cishou (Master Shen).
Shen, in turn, nudged him with his elbow to face him. The Master then summoned Shan and said to him: "That which you asked about, Master Cheng, is insufficient."
I thank the great Chan masters for their response; only the junior Elder of Jingyin can resolve the Dharma Master’s doubts. As for those five teachings:
the teaching of the foolish Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is the doctrine of existence; the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna is the doctrine of emptiness;
the final teaching of the Mahāyāna is the doctrine of neither existence nor emptiness; and as for what is called the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna—
This is precisely the meaning of being both existent and empty. What is called the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle is the meaning of being empty yet not non-existent, and existent yet not empty.
This one shout of mine is not only able to penetrate the five teachings;
it can even penetrate all the various schools of the secular world, the hundred philosophers, and all arts and crafts. Then he shouted, "Do you hear it? Shan replied, "I hear it. Cheng—
Cheng said: "Since you have heard it, then this one shout exists; this is that which can lead one into the Hinayana teachings.
He then called out to Shan, "Do you hear me now? Shan replied, "I do not hear it. Cheng said, "Since you do not hear it, then the previous shout was non-existent;
this is that which can lead one into the initial teaching of the Mahayana. When I first uttered the shout, you said there was sound; yet once the shout has long since faded, the sound—

"Extinguish it. You say again that it can be 'Way' and you say it is 'not Way. If it were 'not Way,' then originally it would have truly existed. If it were 'Way,' then at this very moment it would truly not exist.
Since it is neither existent nor non-existent, one is able to enter the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*). When I utter the shout, existence is not existence; it is existence because of non-existence.
When there is no shout, non-existence is not non-existence; it is non-existence because of existence. Thus, existence and non-existence are simultaneous."

Entering the Sudden Teaching: This single shout of mine does not function as a mere shout; it transcends existence and non-existence, and both intellectual understanding and conceptualization are forgotten.
When the Way is present, not even a hair’s breadth is established; when the Way is absent, it pervades the void horizontally.

Thus, this one shout enters into hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of shouts, and those hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of shouts enter into this one shout—this is what it means to enter the Perfect Teaching.
Shansui bowed his head in prostration and took leave of the Master. The Master called Shansui back again and said:

"From a single word to a single silence, from a single movement to a single stillness—from antiquity to the present, throughout the void of the ten directions, amidst the dense array of myriad phenomena, across the six realms and four modes of birth, through the Buddhas of the three periods and all the sages, regarding the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates, the hundreds of thousands of samādhis, and the immeasurable subtle meanings—all are in accord with the Principle."
The pivot [of awakening] is to realize that one is of one body with heaven, earth, and the myriad things; this is called the *dharmakāya*.
That the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only, and that the four seasons and eight nodes of time are of one essence with the Yin and Yang—this is called the *dharmatā*.

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The *dharmatā* pervades all places; whether with form or without form, in a single sound or a single color, it is entirely contained within a single mote of dust. Within this, it contains all.
The four meanings—the phenomena and the principle—are boundless, pervasive without exception, intermingled yet not confused, and blended yet not one.

All of these are fully contained within this single shout. This is still merely the establishment of a gate for transformation and instruction, a skillful means according to capacity, termed a "small resting place" where one has not yet reached the Precious Abode.
Little do they realize that beneath the gate of our patriarchal masters, mind was transmitted through mind and the Dharma...
The Dharma of the seal does not rely on written words; it is to see one's nature and become a Buddha. There exists a supreme path that has not been transmitted by a thousand sages.
Shan asked again, "What is the path that goes downward? Cheng said, "For now, you should understand it by going downward."
Shan said, "What is this 'treasure place'? Cheng replied, "It is not within your sphere of experience. Shan said, "I hope the Chan Master will show me his compassion.
Cheng said, "Let the vast ocean change as it may; I shall never explain it for you. Thereupon, Shan was silenced and his spirit was disheartened;

his countenance changed with a look of distress, and he withdrew in shame and embarrassment. Alas! Cheng’s learning was vast and his realization of the Way profound; he encountered the source in every direction.

Seizing this opportunity, he shattered their arrogance before the assembly of devas and humans; even if the former masters had supported the school, they could have added nothing more significant than this.
During the Yuanfeng era, Chan Master Yuquan Hao led the assembly at Guyin in Xiangyang, his reputation towering above all quarters.
The Layman Wujin, Zhang Gong, while on an official mission to the Jingzhou and Southwest circuits, went to visit him. He asked, "Under whom did you receive the Dharma?
Huìhào replied, "Under Master Guang of Beita in Fuzhou. The Layman said, "May I hear what kind of accord you had with him?
Huìhào said, "It was precisely because he refused to explain it thoroughly to others. The Layman appreciated these words and subsequently invited him to establish the Dharma.
At Dayang in Jingzhou, the abbot of Guyin was privately delighted, thinking that his head seat would now emerge into the world;

he gathered a great assembly of monastics and laypeople, filled with admiration. Daoyu Hao ascended the seat and said, "I, Hao, have been at Guyin for ten years, yet I have never drunk a single drop of Guyin’s water nor chewed a single grain of Guyin’s rice. If you do not understand this, come to Dayang."

"I shall explain it for you and break it apart," he said, and taking up his staff, he descended from the seat and departed with an air of arrogance. He subsequently moved to Yüan-ch'uan, where he addressed the assembly, saying:

"One night the rain poured down in torrents, knocking over the grape arbor. The administrators, the heads of departments, the novices, and the laborers—those who were leaning leaned, and those who were propping propped.
Propping and leaning, they did so until daybreak; yet, as before, they remain pitiable. He himself considered this [to be the ultimate teaching].
The verse praises matters pertaining to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). As Master Fu Da-shi said: "Empty-handed, I hold a hoe. Dongshan said:
"On Mount Wutai, clouds steam the rice. These only praise matters pertaining to the side of the Dharma-body. Nevertheless, his way of being was transcendent and unrestrained;
he was not easily to be judged by the standards of ordinary or sage. He once fashioned a loincloth, inscribed the names of the patriarchs of successive generations upon it, and wore it, saying:
"Only Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are slightly superior. I shall write this upon my sash. Thus, the monastic community came to refer to him as "Hao the White Drawers.
A serving monk imitated him; Hao saw this and rebuked him, saying, "What principles do you possess that you dare to treat this as a mere joke?
It will be too late when you vomit blood. The monk subsequently passed away at Lumen, just as Hao had said. Alas!
That which is shared by the world and that which is distinct from the Way are merely its traces. As for Huishao’s proclamation of the Way, it opened up and clarified right view;
yet as for his manifestations being extraordinary, they were unfathomable. If one seeks him among those of the past, he was likely a peer to the likes of Deng Yinpeng and Puhua.
When Huanglong Zhongdao first arrived at Longmen in Shuzhou, he took a stroll by the water mill and saw a sign that read:
"The Dharma Wheel Turns Constantly. Suddenly, he attained realization. Clapping his hands, he spoke this verse: "Turning the Great Dharma Wheel—enveloped within the present moment."
He asked again, "How is it? [Foguo] replied, "Water pushes stones; a millstone grinds. He then drew a circle and presented it. Later, he went to the Abbot’s quarters to show it to Chan Master Fuyan.
Afterward, he took his leave and crossed the Nine Rivers to ascend Mount Lu. There he slept in the open air and lodged in the grass, with snakes and tigers as neighbors.

Where the mountains were expansive and the waters slow, he would settle once he had attained realization of the meaning. Sometimes he would not eat for several days, or remain through consecutive nights without sleep.

He did not lie down to sleep; he did not cut his long hair; and he did not change his worn-out robes. For these reasons, those at the Chan assembly respectfully called him a "Loyal Wayman" (Zhongdao).
At that time, Master Sīti (Sīxin) resided at Huanglong, where his reputation was preeminent in the age. As students arrived, there was no room for them all.

Therefore, the retreat was established in the final month of spring to limit those who might join. Sī-mind’s countenance was stern and his moral authority awe-inspiring; few dared to encounter his sharp edge.

Zhōngzhí stepped forward to oppose him with a discourse, offering a verse in his style that said: "Do not blame this mad monk for cursing Sī-mind; Sī-mind, by establishing the summer retreat, has ruined the monastic grove.
If you of the monastic grove possess clear eyes and entrust yourselves to me, This speech must be made to circulate through all time. Furthermore:
As dusk approached, he took a sword made of white wood, went to his room, and asked, "I have heard that the Old Monk does not fear birth and death;
is this true? Sishin intended to respond, but Zhong immediately brandished the sword. Sishin extended his neck and laughed. Zhong threw the sword to the ground, performed a dance, and departed.
The Imperial Censor Feng Jichuan once submitted a petition requesting Zhong to reside at Shengye Monastery; it read in brief: [The text continues with the petition.]
Under the guidance of Foyan, he polished his head; within the chamber of Sishin, he allowed the sword of wisdom to be brandished.
This is considered by the world to be an authentic record.
Chan Master Zifu Shan of Fuzhou was a native of Gutian. His surname was Chen. From his youth, he possessed a spirit of transcendence.
He received the tonsure at Baofeng Monastery and immediately crossed the ridges to attend upon Chan Master Ciming of Shishuang.

At that time, even such eminent masters as Master Zhen of Cuoyan were humbled by him; thus, the monastic communities throughout the land came to know the reputation of Attendant Shan. When [he went] to pay his respects...
Ciming sent Cishi back to Min. As he was departing, Ciming improvised a verse for him, saying: "Seven-fold rice gruel; a sesame cake from the oven.
From this parting, the sledgehammer falls into the well. Subsequently, Cishi appeared in the world at Fenglin in the village, and later moved to Zifuku, where he remained obscure and left no mark.
Consequently, his words and phrases rarely circulated in the world. He possessed the Three Mysterious Essentials (San Xuan Yao).
The verse of the secret instruction says: "The Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials, along with the Three Instructions— How can the Chan practitioners of the four seas distinguish them?
In the land of Aparagoyānī they clamor and shout; In Uttarakuru the people forge iron. What could Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna have said?
Maitreya and Vajrapāṇi both bite their tongues. Mañjuśrī laughs loudly: 'A-he-he! Kāśyapa wishes to speak, yet cannot speak. Speak!
"No. The old Śākyamuni’s beard and whiskers have turned white; his hair has turned white. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Again, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"Leisurely cast forth the three-inch blade, its edge sharp and keen; ice and frost pervade the earth as the rules of order are established.
If you possess the true spirit of a man of honor, let you strike out and manifest your brilliance at will. Second, he said: "The hook is lowered into the four seas, where waves engulf it."

Rarely encountered is a fierce dragon stirring its horns and scales; a lion’s snarl fully reveals its spirit. Amidst this纵横 (zōnghéng—unrestricted movement), who can manifest the person of the present?
Alas! Sengshan was in the same rank as Huanglong, Yangqi, and Cuiyan; moreover, he had long been among these masters.
His style of discourse and fundamental intent were also excellent. Why would he have returned to his hometown? Had he suddenly fallen under the influence of Ciming?
During the Zhenghe era, Chan Master Yuanwu retired from affairs at Zhaojue in Chengdu and again traveled south through the Gorges.
At that time, Zhang Wujin was residing in Jingnan, where he considered himself a master of the Way and was seldom granted high praise by others. Yuanwu moored his boat to pay him a visit.

He engaged in an intense discussion on the essential tenets of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, saying: "The realm of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the *Avataṃsaka* is the total reality of both principle and phenomena;

there is not the slightest element of artificiality therein. Thus, within the one, there are the myriad, and the myriad are understood as the one. One follows upon one, and the myriad follows upon the myriad—vast and inexhaustible.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are non-different in these three aspects. Their unfolding and rolling up are spontaneous and free, unimpeded and perfectly interfused. Although this...
"The ultimate limit is, in the end, merely ripples on a windless sea. At this, the Master (Dongshan) unconsciously drew his seat closer.

Yuanwu then asked, "At this point, is it the same as or different from the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "I am asking you. Yuanwu replied, "That still has nothing to do with it.
The Master’s expression turned sullen. Yuanwu said, "Have you not seen Yunmen say: 'The mountain...'"

"The great earth and the rivers have not the slightest fault; yet this is still a turning phrase (*zhuǎnjù*). Only when one reaches the point where not a single form (*yī sè*) is seen does it constitute a partial presentation (*bàntí*).
One must further know that there is a time for the full presentation (*quántí*) beyond this. Were not Deshan and Linji such full presentations? The Master nodded his head in agreement.

The following day, he again raised the matter of the "Dharma-realm of phenomena" (*shì fǎjiè*) and the "Dharma-realm of principle" (*lǐ fǎjiè*), up to the point of "the non-duality of phenomenon and principle" (*lǐshì wú'èr*).
[The Master] said, "It is obstructed by the dharma-realm. Yuanwu asked again, "Can this be called Chan? The Master replied, "It is precisely the right time to speak of Chan.
Yuanwu laughed and said, "Not so. This is still within the measure of the dharma-realm. As long as the measure of the dharma-realm has not been extinguished, it is not yet possible to speak of Chan.
Only when one reaches the dharma-realm of non-obstruction in all things and the measure of the dharma-realm is extinguished can one truly speak of Chan. What is the Buddha? A dry piece of dung."
[The Master] struck the pillar with his staff. "What is the Buddha? "Three catties of hemp. Therefore, Zhenjing’s verse says:

"In every matter there is no obstruction; one acts with sovereign ease. Holding a pig's head in hand, one recites the pure precepts in the mouth. Chasing [the pig] out of the brothel, yet not having yet repaid the wine debt.
At the crossroads, he unties the sack. The Duke said, "How magnificent this discourse! How could it be easily heard? Indeed, Yuanwu..."

The harmonious integration of the various teachings is such as this; thus, those who have attained realization find their hearts gladdened and submit with sincerity. Were it not for one who is proficient in both the doctrine and its exposition, how could this be possible?
Master Nan of Xiaoshan, an Arhat of Mount Lu, was the son of the Zhang family of Tingzhou. The Jinquan Temple south of the prefecture was his [monastery].
He resided at Daolin Monastery on Mount Tan, where he studied under Chan Master Daoxuan Zhaoyou and received his seal of approval (*yinke*).

He subsequently moved to Luohan Monastery, where he served as the head of the Hall Administration (*tangsi*) and was appointed to share the master’s seat (*fenzuo*). When Zhaoyou moved to Yunju, he succeeded him there, and his reputation became preeminent throughout all quarters.
Students flocked to him in great numbers. At that time, there was a lay practitioner named Zhang Jie who was deeply intent on investigating the Way.
One day, Nan asked him, "How is it? Zhang replied, "I do not understand. Nan continued to press him without ceasing, until Zhang suddenly grasped the essential meaning.
He immediately responded with a verse, saying: "Heaven does not support me, nor does the earth know me. Who speaks of south, north, east, and west? My body lies upon the Great..."
The ocean takes Mount Sumeru as its pillow; how truly marvelous that stone sprouts have sent forth branches! Zhang Xun requested leave to depart, and Nan showed him two verses, saying:
"When you reach Mount Lu, Mount Lu will come to you; who else but you shall go to my Mount Lu? Go out the gate and ask the wind atop the ridge:
the Great Way flows freely, with no foundation to rely upon. He further said: "Head clad in a black cap, wearing a white robe... (The text continues with the mountain).
I lend you a year’s leisure in my quarters. Stepping out the door, I shall tell you the path by which you came: your home lies amidst the verdant mists of Huangpo.
As for Luohan Zhun, his lineage traces back to Huanglong as his great-grandfather;

since their names were identical, his reputation for the Way nearly rivaled that of the elder, and thus the monastic community referred to him as "Little Nan" (Xiaonan), while honoring Huanglong as "Old Nan" (Laonan). Nevertheless, Luohan was dedicated to the transmission of the Dharma.

After seven years had passed, he remained in the world for forty-three years. Although his full potential was not yet fully realized, his brilliant reputation was established during his own time and has been celebrated by posterity;
thus, Yunju may truly be said to have had a worthy son.
Chan Master Dajue formerly resided at Letan. While sitting in meditation within his chamber, he saw a golden serpent emerge from the ground;

after a short while, it vanished. Those who heard of this praised it as an auspicious omen. Not long thereafter, he traveled from Yuan Tong on Mount Lu to take up residence at Jingyin Monastery in the Eastern Capital by imperial decree.
Previously, when Emperor Renzong was reading the recorded sayings of Touzi, he reached the point where a monk asked: "What is the Unconcealed?"
Dizang addressed him as "White Ox of the Earth. Touzhi rebuked him with a series of shouts. Through this, Dizang attained awakening and composed fourteen verses on the Buddhist scriptures;
here we record only the first: "If you ask about the Lord of the House, True stillness merges with the vast void. Three heads and six arms— In the twelfth month, it is truly spring breeze.
He then presented these to Huilian, who offered this response: "If you ask about the Lord of the House, It is limpid and clear..."

It resembled the azure void; clouds and thunder occasionally stirred, and the heavens and earth were entirely filled with a harmonious breeze. Having entered [the palace], he spent the second watch of the night in study. The Emperor bestowed upon him a dragon-brain (kunkuma) bowl.
After Lia finished expressing his gratitude, he took up the bowl and said, "In our Dharma, one wears dyed robes and eats from vessels of clay or iron.

This bowl is not in accordance with the Dharma. He then burned it. When the imperial messenger returned and reported this, the Emperor’s heart was greatly pleased. After some time, he submitted another memorial.

The verse for requesting to return to the mountains says: For six years in the imperial capital, I chanted the Patriarch’s pivot; Twice in the golden halls, I received the Emperor’s majesty. Now departing to hide among the green mountains, what joy could be greater?
I shall return with nothing but the Imperial Verses filling my satchel. The Imperial Response says: The Buddhas and Patriarchs clearly manifest the supreme pivot;

Only by realizing it before the pivot does one fully possess its majesty. The green mountains are the *prajñā* of the *tathatā* (suchness) body; These Imperial Verses shall be collected [as a record].

"Where shall I return? He then offered another verse in thanks, saying: "The Imperial Messenger has proclaimed my release from the forbidden precincts, Yet bids me once more dwell within these Zen gates.
The green mountains refuse to hide a thousand follies; With white hair, how can I serve the myriad affairs of state?

The grace of rain and dew remains deep and vast, While my attachment to forest and spring is bitter and lingering. How much more so, the benevolence of Yao is as expansive as heaven— I shall simply let things be."
Like a solitary cloud, he flies at his own will. During the Zhizhi period, he submitted a memorial requesting to return home. Emperor Ying bestowed upon him an official edict, stating:
"The Chan Master Huailian of Dajue has received the sacred favor of the late Emperor; he has been repeatedly granted imperial writings and has frequently presented his sincere devotion."

He requested to return to the forest hermitages; now his request is granted, so that he may fulfill his desire for leisure. Whenever he passes by minor monasteries, he shall reside there according to his inclination.
As for the great monasteries of the ten directions, they must not constrain him with insistent invitations. When Liaan took him eastward back home, few knew of it.

When Su Shi, the Hanlin Academician, was serving as Governor of Hangzhou, he sent a letter inquiring after him, saying: "I understand you have been commissioned to compose the *Chenqi* (Imperial Calligraphy)."
The Inscription for the Pavilion has been respectfully completed. Being frail and having long neglected my studies, I do not know whether it is fit to be engraved upon stone.

I heard from Chan Master Canliao that when he left the capital, Emperor Ying bestowed upon him a handwritten edict. Its purport stated, in brief: "To reside and preside according to one's own nature. I wonder if this is indeed the case?
If so, I earnestly request that you provide the full text, for I wish to include this passage here. I, Lian, [humbly] conclude.
It was concealed and not brought forth until, following the passing of the one who had entrusted it to him in accordance with the Way, it was recovered from his chest and casket.

That it did not shine forth prematurely is sufficient to cause those who rely on power and harbor their own favor to blush with shame. As for the late Renzong Emperor, during the leisure between his myriad state affairs, he engaged in poetic exchange with Liaan, elucidating the essential vehicle of the Buddha to support his supreme governance;
thus, the inscription for the Chenshui Pavilion states that he attained the Dharma of the Buddha-mind, a distinction shared by none before or since.
"There is but one person. How true these words are!
When the Duke of Zhongfu was stationed at Bozhou, he welcomed Master Huayan Yong and hosted him at the provincial seat, consulting him on the Dharma of the mind.
Having already attained realization, he later replied in a letter to Huiyong:

"Regarding what you have shown me concerning this matter—that the Buddha must surely have had a prior cause and that it cannot be resolved in this present life—if this is indeed so, yet once I encountered the Venerable Master, I suddenly recognized that which had been forgotten since beginningless time.
From now on, I must certainly pull myself out from the sea of birth and death; it is not a matter of mere seeking."

I have always known this. Although one may exhaust all one's strength to sever it, the Way does not emerge. Even if you, Master, were to find a hundred thousand assistants, what benefit would that be for the matter?
It would be nothing more than finding an old, sickly layman who has emerged from beneath the assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Master Jide has accomplished much; what he says regarding "winnowing" is indeed true.
Whenever I reflect upon the ancient patriarchs, I see that they initially remained with their own teachers for twenty or thirty years, or at the very least, served them for a dozen or so years.
Only after hearing the Way and the Dharma day after day did they finally attain penetration from top to bottom. I then recall how twice I, Bi, received [instruction].
The Master has looked upon me with compassion. Over the course of two months, I have sought his instruction;

yet, how much more intelligence could I have attained, and how much effort could I have applied, were it not for the Master’s skillful means in providing expedient guidance and exerting himself to awaken me? Otherwise, by what means could I have seen the limits of the Way?
Though I were to grind my bones to powder and shatter my body, there would be no way to repay your kindness. I do not know on what day I shall again be able to behold you in person; I can only—
Day and night, he remained devotedly attached [to his teacher]. Alas! The Buddhas of the past specifically stated that it is difficult for those of wealth and status to study the Way;

how much more so for one who has reached the pinnacle of nobility among ministers, who, seizing the opportunity of fame and merit, has achieved such accomplishment—this is truly the most difficult of all.
To record this on bamboo slips and silk, he reverently honors Master Yong, declaring that this is no ordinary act of gratitude; how could he be deceiving others?

Chan Master Yuanzhao Ben was naturally sincere and lacked any artificial refinement. When he first traveled to Yunju, several friends were viewing the Stone Drum together and had encouraged one another to compose verses on it.
Some remarked that Ben had never applied himself to the brush and inkstone, so they playfully compelled him to do so.
Ben immediately composed this verse: "The work of creation is accomplished beyond measure; One cannot calculate its kalpas nor fathom its years. Like..."
"Now he lies across the solitary peak; his understanding of the subtle sound pervades the great thousandfold world. His peers were struck with astonishment at this.
He then went to visit Chan Master Huai at Jingde Temple in Chiyang. Once he had received the Master’s instruction, he lived and worked among the community without anyone knowing it.
One day, Huai posed a question, saying: "The long night in the hells is a suffering that pains the heart of anyone who hears of it. Devadatta is there..."

"In the midst of hell, how can one instead obtain the bliss of the third dhyāna heaven? Since no one present could provide a fitting response, Huai said, "This must be answered with words from the Master himself.
He then hurriedly summoned Ben, who arrived. Huai posed the previous question to him. Ben replied, "Karma lies within it.
From that moment on, the entire assembly changed their perspective. Later, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Hui-lin Monastery, where his Way accorded perfectly with the Emperor's.
His reputation spread throughout the world, and his words regarding the "rare sounds" pervading the great trichiliocosm—how could these have been merely superficial?
During the Mingdao era, Chan Master Song of Mingjiao borrowed books from the family collection of the Ouyang clan of Xishan in Yuzhang and studied them at Fengsheng Monastery;
he subsequently integrated the Buddhist five precepts and ten wholesome actions with the five [constants] of Confucianism.
He took "The Constant" as the fundamental teaching of his school. At that time, the Duke Ou-yang Hsiu admired Han Yü’s exclusion of Buddhism, and Li Tai-po of Hsing-chiang followed in his tradition.
Ch’ung therefore took his writings and visited Li Tai-po three times to discuss the perfect harmony between Confucianism and Buddhism, even challenging his assertions.
Li Tai-po appreciated the loftiness of his prose and was convinced by the superiority of his reasoning; he consequently sent him a letter.

He praised Qisong to Wen Zhonggong. Subsequently, while residing at Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou, he composed the *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage) and the *Dingzutú* (Chart of the Determined Patriarchs).
He carried these to the capital and submitted a formal petition at the Kaifeng Prefecture. Prefect Wang Gong Su, styled Zhongyi, presented them to the Emperor with a memorial, stating:
"Your servant now has the monk Qisong of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou, who has come through your servant to submit a petition, claiming that [the Chan lineage]..."

The transmission of the Dharma within the ancestral lineage of our school was not yet clearly defined. Those of shallow learning in the teaching tradition each clung to their own records, leading to much contention throughout past and present.
Therefore, I have thoroughly investigated the Tripitaka to fully ascertain the origins and developments of the ancestral masters of the Chan school.

Consequently, I have edited out the superfluous and extracted the essentials, composing the *Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma* in twelve fascicles, along with an illustrated chart of the patriarchs.
[The Emperor] said: "Because the *Zhengzhuanji* contains errors, I have commissioned you to annotate the printed edition of the *Fujiaobian* in three volumes and submit a letter to His Majesty.
This is not to solicit any favor or grace; I merely request that Your Majesty accept my submission.

Having applied myself somewhat to the teachings of Buddhism, I have observed the revisions and annotations [in this work]; thus, it is not based on mere conjecture. It is quite refined and precise. Regarding the myriad affairs of state, Your Majesty..."
In my leisure time, I have deeply attained the joy of the Dharma. I pray that Your Majesty will deign to examine this;

if there is anything worthy of adoption, I beg that it be submitted to the Chongju (Central Secretariat) for detailed review and that it be specially included in the catalog of the Tripitaka. This is respectfully submitted. When King Inmyeong read the manuscript, he approved the petition.
The imperial edict was sent to the Secretariat (Zhongshu). Prime Minister Han Wei Gong and State Councilor Ouyang Wenzhong Gong examined it together;

they marveled at its scriptural investigations and textual corroboration, finding no errors whatsoever. Thereupon, the court honored him with the title of Dharma Master Mingjiao and granted the work entry into the Tripitaka.
A memorandum from the Secretariat stated: "Wang Su, acting Governor of Kaifeng, reports that at Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou..."

The monk Qisong has composed the *Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma* (*Chuanfa Zhengzong Ji*) and the *Supplementary Collection for the Edification of the Teachings* (*Fujiao Bian*) in three fascicles.

An order was issued to the Translation Court (*Chuandefa Yuan*) to include these within the Tripitaka. A formal memorandum was sent to the Translation Court: "In accordance with this, the eminent writings and profound treatises of Qisong [are hereby included]."
It is sufficient to serve as a medium for proclaiming the Great Transformation.

Now that it has been presented to the throne and admitted into the Great Canon, the merit of upholding the framework of the Dharma will never grow old, even with the passing of days and months. Alas! Among our own ranks, there are those who have not set eyes upon it throughout their entire lives.
How could one know the source of these hidden benefits and silent advantages?
The Chan Master Pu, a monk from Shu, styled himself the Abbot of Xingkong Hermitage. He studied under the Chan Master Sīxīn and resided at Huátíng for the longest time.
He was particularly fond of playing the iron flute, living in carefree joy beyond the reach of either sages or ordinary people. He was also skilled in composing verses.
He guided people, saying: "When mind and dharmas are both forgotten, one is still separated by delusion; when form and emptiness are non-dual, a trace of dust remains.

The hundred birds do not come and spring passes once more; I know not who is the person dwelling in the hermitage. He further warned the assembly, saying: "Studying the Way is like guarding a forbidden city:
by day, one wards off the six thieves; by night, one remains alert. Only when the commander-in-chief of the central army can carry out his orders [is the city secure]."
"Without moving a blade of grass, bring about Great Peace. He also said: "Eating without plowing and wearing clothes without sericulture;

pure and leisurely beyond the mundane world, one finds fulfillment in this sagely age. Yet, if you have not yet passed through the pivot of the Patriarch’s gate, you must still intentionally seek an advantage.
He further said: "In the twelve hours of the day, do not let your work cease. Examine, examine until it reaches the infinite. You must penetrate thoroughly to the very bottom of that infinity."
He trampled down the highest peak of Mount Sumeru. Chan Master Xuedou Chishi once offered a verse in response, saying:

"How joyful is the Elder Xingkong! He possesses nothing but three robes and a single bowl. A true son of the forest who has died his heart out— Seeing through with courage, his discourse is expansive and clear.
Sometimes he blows the flute as his teaching; With a single blast, he causes the moon over the West River to fall."
In the joyful moments within the Peach Blossom Hermitage, those who observe often fail to reach the point of the dance. What profound principle can truly bring such delight?
Waving his hand toward others, he responds with a parting word; yet it is laughable that no one understands this meaning.
Everyone says the hammer is as hard as iron; only those of the true lineage cannot be deceived. To inform you: do not let it leak when the moment arrives. Thus, he wished to pursue the boat.
Regarding the story of Master Shi: he said, "To die while sitting or standing is not as good as a water burial. First, it saves firewood; second, it avoids opening a grave.
To cast off one's hands and go forth is truly exhilarating. Who is the true connoisseur? It is Master Chuanzi.
His lofty style is difficult to emulate after a thousand years; few people sing his single song of the fisherman. He then addressed the assembly, saying, "Master Chuanzi..."
Returning to his hometown in his later years, his traces vanished; his wondrousness was difficult to measure. His true style was uniquely inherited by those who shared his realization;
he played his iron flute crosswise as the performance concluded. He then said to the monastics and laypeople, "I am departing.

Thereupon, upon the Qīnglóng River, he mounted a wooden basin, unfurled a cloth sail, and blew his iron flute, drifting far away until he disappeared. When Hǔchí heard that he had transformed into water, he composed a verse:
He lamented him, saying: "Neither monk nor layman, neither worldly nor secular; he once received the direct entrustment of Sīxīn.
Throughout his life he knew his destiny and wandered at ease; he practiced the Way but lacked pure blessings. East, west, south, and north, he let loose his folly and stupidity;
for seventy-seven years he was full of strange antics. He has entered the lacquer bucket and bathed in the waves—who among them understands the birthless?"
Song: Flowing with the current, it goes and flows back again. Is it not that before the hermitage he yearns for his bamboo staff?
A-he-he! This old brother is happy; who can do anything to him? Alas! The matter of birth and death is truly great, yet he treats it as a game.
This is no empty talk. Observing what he preserves within, how could one possibly debate it?
Chan Master Xiaoshou of Mount Gui and Chan Master Dashou of Fayun had long relied upon Master Tianyi Huai;
they were known as "thoroughly cultivated" students and both possessed great reputations, such that the monastic community referred to them as the "Great and Small [Shous].
Consequently, they traveled together to visit various regions, first calling upon Master Yuanjian Yuan at Mount Fu. Yuan wished to recruit them, so he presented them with a verse and...
He compiled the *Jiudan ji* (Collection of Nine Strands of the Chan Gate) and admonished it, saying: "Were it not for those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence, how could one speak of this?
Da Xiu secretly grasped his intention and immediately composed a verse in response: "Who can comb their hair twice in a single day? Once the base of the topknot is secured, they may stop.
For the most part, it is simply because their natural frame is fine; Without applying rouge or powder, they remain elegant. At that time...
Chan Master Nan resided at Jicui Hermitage on Huangbo Mountain.
Upon hearing a monk cite the words of the "Three Barriers," Xiaoxiu was struck with awe and wonder, and wished to go see him. Daxiu said, "I have no further doubts. Thereupon, Xiaoxiu set out alone.
Fearing that Xiaoxiu might not return, Daxiu secretly ordered a monk to observe Master Nan’s conduct. After a month had passed, the monk saw him sitting in solitude.
He remained as still as a single mat. Upon returning, he told Daxiu, "This old man has no other special talent; he is merely a monk who practices the Way.
Because of this, Daxiu yielded to Xiaoxiu, saying, "This scholar lost his guard midway and has betrayed our late master.
Subsequently, Daxiu traveled to the banks of the Huai River and led the assembly of monks at Baiyun, where Master Duan took up the position.
Mount Shisi (Four Sides) was slightly more prominent than Huangbo. After a long time, he attained realization. Hearing that Dashi had moved to Qixian, he sent him a verse, saying:
"In this field of dharma where seven hundred eminent monks fought, Master Lu’s single verse caused them all to surrender.
No one could block the road to Huangmei; I was forced to travel far across the Nine Rivers. Furthermore, he once composed a verse on the "Three Barriers" dialogue, saying: "I..."

The Buddha’s hand is the hand of the practitioner; who does not possess it? To use it clearly and directly—why must one run about in madness? My feet are donkey-feet; they tread upon high and low alike.

When the rain has passed, the moss is green; when the clouds part, the sun blazes. When asked about my origins, I have no doubts anywhere. My words are straightforward and my mind is free from ailment;
who would argue over right and wrong? Xiaoxiu was the son of the Ying family of Yiyang. His family lineage had been engaged in the study of Confucianism for generations.
Huanʼan Yuan was his former residence. If Da-xiu, following the words of others, had remained ignorant of the Master at Jicui and instead relied upon Baiyun, he would have truly made a wise choice.
Xiao-xiu, harboring doubts regarding the "Three Barriers" dialogue, sought a definitive resolution from him.
Truly, he did not deceive himself. Thereafter, both [he and his predecessor] served as the leaders of the Dharma path; how could their decisions and selections be subject to criticism?
Chan Master Yuan of Huguo Temple in Taizhou was popularly known within the monastic community as "Yuan the Bagman. He first went to study under Ciyun Wuzu Fayan.
While at Mount Jangshan, the Master heard a monk reciting the words from Sīxin’s informal discourse: "Since one is deluded, one must attain awakening;

since one has awakened, one must recognize delusion within awakening and awakening within delusion. When both delusion and awakening are forgotten, one establishes all dharmas from the place where there is neither delusion nor awakening.
Hearing this, he was struck with doubt and immediately proceeded to the Buddha hall. Reaching out his hand to push open the door-panels, he experienced a sudden, expansive realization.

Dacheng subsequently served Huianwu as an attendant. His intellectual discernment and eloquence were exceptionally brilliant. Because Huianwu spoke in the Sichuan dialect, he dubbed Dacheng "Nautou" (The Headless One).
Attendant Yuan then inscribed his own portrait and presented it to him, saying: "Throughout my life, I have spoken only of 'Nautou Zen.
When one encounters a Nautou, it is like hitting an iron wall. Casting off the cage, the heels are severed; Even if the entire earth were gathered together, it would be as pitch-black as ink."
In his later years, he again submerged the "diao" and "dao" [of conventional terminology]. Wielding the vajra mallet, he shattered the nests and dens.

If you wish to recognize the face of Yuanwu at another time, I shall extract it for him all at once. When Yuanwu returned to Shu, Yuan went back to Zhe-dong, where he polished away his brilliance and buried his light.

He did not seek fame or renown. Provincial Governor of Kuāngcáng, Gěng Yǎnxī, had previously sought the Way from Yuánwù and had read through his recorded sayings up to the section on the portrait inscriptions;
thus, he came to understand Yuan’s character. He subsequently invited him to open the Dharma at Nánkāishān and dispatched an envoy to search for him as far as Bào’ēn Monastery in Tái.
There, he found him in the communal quarters and urged him to accept the mandate. It was then that Fāngzhàng Gǔgōng...
The eminent disciples of Lingyuan, upon hearing his proclamations, were likewise deeply struck by their extraordinary nature. From this, one can see the reach of his influence at that time:

dragons and elephants trod together, and even those like Yuan Gao and Dao Shang gathered in groups. Having perfected his inner cultivation, he emerged when the times were right; thus he stood preeminent in the world.
As for those today who possess jade within but only the appearance of jade on the outside and are anxious to sell themselves, let them look to the conduct of Yuan as their standard.
Li: "Can one not be free from shame?
Master Lingsuan had early on studied under Huitang at Huanglong, and the fame of his attendant, Qing, was renowned throughout the monastic community.
In the seventh year of the Yuanyou era, the layman Zhang Gong, known as Wujin, served as the Commissioner for Jiangxi and thus came to admire him deeply. This...

At that time, Lingyuan was residing at Xinghua. The authorities issued a formal decree to the magistrate of Fening, ordering him to join with the abbots of various mountains to invite him to take up the position at Guanyin Monastery in Yuzhang.
The command was extremely strict, and having no choice, he personally went out to offer a verse of refusal:

"Without a single inch of land, I am as poor as a needle through bone; In benefiting sentient beings, I deeply regret lacking further treasures. Within the marketplace, the great gate of giving is difficult to open."

"I beg to retire to the green mountains to nourish my sickly body. When Huang Dashi Luzu was living in seclusion within his native village, he sent a handwritten note to the Elder Hai of Xinghua, saying:
"I have heard that the seat of Guanyin is vacant and that the higher authorities have a strong interest in you, Brother Qing.
It would be quite well indeed if Brother Qing were determined not to go; the peach of immortality ripens only once every three thousand years—do not act like a faded-flower almond."
Set this aside. Huanglong and Xinghua would also have acted as conditions for aiding the Path;
they worked together with one arm. Do not let others climb the tree and then pull out the ladder! Alas! During the Yuanyou era, the Dharma-way of Jiangxi flourished;
those who presided over the monasteries were indeed high-souled in their vision. Moreover, the rites of selection were as exceptionally distinguished as this. Lingyuan expressed it in verse:
He declined the offer with great earnestness, yet the Grand Historian praised him in his records. Was this not said because he was moved by some profound inspiration?
Linqiong was appointed as the Head Seat again; he had a flat head and deep-set eyes, and though short and slight, he was vigorous and resolute.

He frequently traveled between the mountains of Huai, where Master Baiyun Chuan held him in high esteem. One day, while they were out walking in the mountains, Baiyun spoke as they went, saying: "You..."

"Have you ever met any venerable masters? Try telling me about them. He replied, "Recently, while in Huxiang, I had the fortune of personally relying upon Master Ya of Fuyan, Master Peng of Shangfeng, and Master Xian of Beichen. Baoyun said, "So you have indeed met true adepts!
But let me ask you this: 'Xuansha did not go beyond the ridge'—what is the meaning of this? He then stepped forward and took hold of Baoyun's whisk.
Yunshou gave a single pinch. Baoyun asked again, "How was it when Lingyun saw the peach blossoms and attained enlightenment?
He then immediately kicked him over and said, "I thought you were a man! Baoyun sprang up and simply smiled.
From that time on, he was held in high esteem by the monastic community; even Wuzu Yan Heshang treated him as a fatherly elder and had Foyan personally study his discourses.

what need is there to discuss whether one is the person of old or not? Later, while residing at Fuyan Hermitage in Lianjiang County, I found myself burdened by a large number of dependents and so pressed for time that I had no leisure.

In the third year of the Yuanyou era, Chan Master Foyan was returning from Feichuan after begging for alms at Taitang in Shuzhou.
At that time, he was twenty-one years old, and as Master Yan was about to depart for Haihui, Foyan said with deep emotion: "My service..."

Having just crossed the river, he again accompanied [the Master] to a desolate monastery. How could An possibly investigate and resolve his own matter? He then composed a verse to take his leave, saying:
"From here to the road of Min and E, five thousand li lie westward. Fortunate to have carried my bottle and staff to pay homage to the High Chan Master.

Though I am unskilled, I have often seen you wield the axe; Yet with dull feet, it is hard to follow as you raise the whip again. I deeply feel your grace, like the sun and moon, But I am unable to keep pace."
His traces shall rest in the forests and springs; tomorrow morning you shall depart from the mountains. We shall have the opportunity to meet again in days to come. Yuan sent him off with this verse:
When we parted before the Wanzhe Terrace, The peach blossoms were like brocade, the willows like eyebrows.
On this day next year, leaning against the railing to look, I shall see as before but one or two green branches. Foyan sat out the summer retreat at Jiangshan. By chance...

When he met Master Linyuan, his friendship grew increasingly deep. During a relaxed conversation, Foyan said, "Recently, I have seen that a certain venerable master in the capital seems to have a karmic affinity with you.
Linyuan replied, "Master Yan is a peerless patriarch in this world;
why would I abandon him to travel so far? Foyan continued, "The one you call 'having an affinity' is merely a teacher of intellectual understanding, whereas you—"

It was only through his initial correspondence that Foyan attained what he had been striving for; he proceeded directly to the oceanic assembly (the monastic community). It was seven years later before he finally grasped the essential meaning. Alas!
Had Foyan lacked even a slight spark of spiritual insight, he would surely have fallen into stagnant water. How could he have managed to pass through the Dragon Gate once more?
As the former masters said, "Those who perfect me are my friends"—how could they deceive anyone?
Chan Master Bian of Heshan in Huzhou traveled to Shaolin in the Western Capital.
There he heard a monk cite a poem by Chan Master Fuyan of Longmen to clarify the story of King Kapphina of Kaśmīra slaying the Venerable Siṃhabhadra:
"By the Yangzi River, willows bloom in spring; Willow catkins bring sorrow to those crossing the river. At twilight on the farewell pavilion, a single blast of the broken flute— O traveler..."

"Facing toward Xiao and Xiang, I head toward Qin. With this, he had a silent realization. He immediately went to Longmen to observe the summer retreat. Before long, Foyan brought up the previous story and questioned him.
As Bian was about to respond, Foyan pushed him away with his hand. Bian stepped out, whereupon he attained a sudden and great enlightenment.
He returned to disclose his realization, but Foyan grabbed his staff and chased him away. Shortly thereafter, the monastery sent someone to beg for grain.
Hu. Due to illness, he was unable to travel and consequently returned to Tiāoxī. He built a hermitage at Xiàshān, where he remained for a long time.
