They sat together discussing how "Heaven and Earth are but a single finger" and "the myriad things are but a single horse," continuing on and on without end. Fenbian paid no heed to their arguments.
Ge, becoming suspicious, asked, "What do you, Master, say? Fenbian smiled but did not answer. After a long while, he called out to the Censor in a stern voice. Ge—
He hurriedly assented. Bian said, "The heavens and earth are but one finger; the myriad things are but one horse. Ge Xian exclaimed, "It must be you, Master, for this to be possible!
The guests sat staring in amazement, their respect deepened. This is what is meant by possessing the skillful means of one who brings life.
Is it possible to act in such a manner?
The Abbot Chūn of Huàdù at Línchuān was a preeminent disciple of Master Xiáng of Bǎofēng.

He was thoroughly versed in the Inner Canon and extensively mastered the Outer Vehicles. His noble character and refined elegance are fully evidenced by his own collection of mountain-dwelling poems, numbering several dozen.
I understand. For now, I shall record only these twelve items. In my own clumsy honesty, I know that my path toward the world is far removed;
being sparse, foolish, and frail, I dwell deep within the mountains. My current livelihood consists of nothing else; there is only a single fathom of gnarled branches.

A roof of several rafters overlooks the water and rocks; a single path leads to the gate, where vines and creepers hang. It is because this place is suited for spending my final years that I have come to enjoy it.
The valley clouds will pass by sooner or later. I laugh at myself for being as reckless and wild as Shide; who knows that my dullness and stupidity are like those of Nanquan?

Several times, satiated from eating, I grew weary of wandering the mountains; thus, I simply sleep wherever I am, clothes and all. Without artifice, in quiet detachment, the clouds return to the cave.
A shadow exists, and the clear moon reflects in the pool; this scene is vividly transcendent of the mundane world. Originally perfected and manifest, there is no need for inquiry.
Following one’s person is only the staff that exceeds the head; for a full belly, one relies solely on the broken-legged cauldron.

Where is it best to dispel idleness time and again? Wandering amidst the sounds of water and the hues of mountains. Where the earthen incense burner burns, pure smoke mists the air; when the iron chime is struck—
The morning resonance is cold. A single string of prayer beads, coarse and heavy; held up, its one hundred and eight beads do not deceive. Yanzi’s single gourd was not for the sake of pleasure;
Sima Xiangru’s four walls were not yet the highest state. How can these compare to the true livelihood of a mountain dweller?

From atop the house, the pine resonance pours forth like autumnal waves. A few lines of large characters on *bèiduō* leaves; a single stick of coarse incense at the root of an ancient cypress. The stone—
The chamber is still and the spring day is long; the cuckoo’s cry pierces the village of falling blossoms.

The fisherman and his son sing the Song of Nectar; they compose verses on the Dharma-lamp in the manner of Hanshan. Do not say there is no one to hear you amidst the deep clouds—the myriad phenomena are all clearly known.

Sitting upon the rock, one already feels the chill in one's very marrow; rinsing the mouth with the spring water, one always finds the teeth and gums refreshed. Within this, there is a flavor that causes one to forget [the world].

I return my thoughts to the Buddha. My body grows old; there is nothing left that accords with this state of mind. Sitting in silence within deep crags, tigers have grown tame; walking along ancient streams, I have naturally befriended the gulls.
This is not because I have forgotten worldly functions or severed all thought; it is simply that, having reached old age, I have found rest for the mind.
Fearing the cold, I am too lazy to shave my tangled hair; loving the warmth, I frequently add more firewood to the hearth. My chestnut-colored *kāṣāya* robe hangs in disarray—who could possibly...?
Though his labor was strenuous, he skillfully arranged his life to sing of leisurely ease; one may say he attained this to the ultimate degree.
Were it not for that which he cultivated within himself, who could have been capable of such a thing?

The Layman Qingyi, Pan Xingsi, style name Yanzhi, was initially appointed as County Magistrate of Dehua. When Xu Jian of the same commandery was first enfeoffed as the Governor of Jiangzhou, Pan went to visit him.
Xu Jian failed to show him proper courtesy, so Pan returned home with his calling card and ultimately did not take up his post.
He sought the Way from the Chan Master Nanshan Huanglong and received his seal of approval. He once said: "I am a recluse in a clear world."
Therefore, he styled himself [as such]. Since the Jiayou era, dozens of recommendation petitions had been submitted by high officials and ministers;

he was subsequently summoned from his post as a Military Commissioner’s Assistant in Yinzhou, but he declined and did not accept. He lived in seclusion on the eastern shore of Donghu Lake in Yuzhang, finding delight in the lute and books.
One day, Chan Master Yuan of Qian’an, a senior disciple of Master Nan, visited him while he was in the midst of dusting his lute. Yuan—
[The Master] said, "Even one who is old and aged still plays with a thread and line. [The other] replied, "One must also pluck it so that it rings. Yuan said, "It is not lacking.
[The other] replied, "How many people can truly know the heart? Jiyin inscribed this on his portrait, saying:
"The birthless treasury of Vairocana; the vessel of the Way in Zhendan. To discourse upon the wondrous meaning, he borrows this body as his tongue; to uphold the great thousandfold world..."

With his hands as his ground, his sharp intellectual acuity was no less than that of Pang Yun, yet he understood the Chan of letters; his conduct and withdrawal were much like those of a child, yet he lived during an era of peace and brilliance.
When Emperor Shu (Shenzong) urged him to serve, he could not be persuaded; when Emperor Shen (Huizong) summoned him, he did not rise.
This is what all the scholar-officials of the realm have heard. Yet, how could the Master have been limited to this alone? Alas! The Master...
Regarding his resignation from office to seek the Way, he maintained the integrity of beginning and end;
since Jiyin has thus revealed his hidden virtue and composed this eulogy for him, one may truly say that a single individual has been seen among those who dwell beneath the forest trees.
In the spring of the fourth year of the Xiaoshing era, Master Miaoxi entered Min Province.

Upon arriving at Guangyin Aranya on Gan-zhai Zhou, he had not yet completed his summer retreat when he moved to Yangyu on the sea. He posted a notice in the communal quarters that read: "The former masters have said:
'When poisonous defilements enter the mind-consciousness, it is like oil entering flour; they cannot be removed for kalpas. Nowadays, when you brothers practice Chan..."
It is possible. However, because the poison has penetrated deep into the marrow, you have been persistently thinking that you can attain the Way;

you have merely continued to practice meditation. When your meditation reaches its end and you happen to gain a single phrase, you rejoice. Such people as these, even the Buddha could not save. From now on, you shall be placed on the lower bench;
you must read the sutras and are not permitted to look at miscellaneous texts. Should you violate this, you shall be expelled along with your entire bench.
In the monastery, Alas! At that time, the assembly numbered barely fifty odd members; yet within the span of eight lunar cycles, thirteen attained realization.
This was indeed due to the power of mutual exhortation.
Chan Master Yunju Shun’s secular surname was Hu; he was a native of Yichun.
During the Huangyou era, he resided at Qixian, where his reputation for the Way rivaled that of Master Bao of Guizong, Master Xian of Kaishan, Master Nan of Kuantang, and Master Ne of Yuanthong.
As Chan practitioners interacted with one another, the monastic communities of Mount Lu flourished more than ever before. Not long after, the local magistrate became corrupt;
however, Shun could not bear to use the property of the monastery to cultivate personal ties and secure his position. He subsequently slandered the magistrate, who then confiscated his robes.
Shun then took up residence at Taiping Hermitage. When King Ren heard of his spiritual practice, he again honored him with monastic robes and bestowed upon him a silver alms bowl.
He took charge of Xiexian. Upon entering the monastery, he spoke a verse: "Without cause, I was slandered and unjustly met with misfortune;
For more than half a year, I lived as a layman. Today I return once more to Sanxia Temple; How many will speak well of me, and how many will resent me? Not long after, he moved to Yunju.
His Way became even more honored and his assembly grew increasingly prosperous. He showed a verse to the assembly, saying: "To seek and to follow principle—both are faults. Not..."
The maladies of those who traverse these two paths are likewise so. Who can say what the ultimate point within this is? A poor man beats his breast for a single coin. Alas!
One may incur reproach by offending a provincial governor, yet gain favor by being known to the Son of Heaven. Thus, misfortune and fortune lie side by side.
What more need be said of Shun?
Chan Master Yuan of Gānlù Monastery in Huzhou composed over twenty *yúfǔ* (fisherman’s) lyrics;
yet, that which is widely circulated in the world is but one. It begins: "Originally a lone fisherman of Xiāoxiāng, drifting east, west, north, and south, I hold only..."
A solitary boat serves as his dwelling; it has neither width nor narrowness. He screens the heavens for a canopy and spreads the earth for a mat—a state difficult for others to fathom.
Recently, I heard that the four seas have laid down their weapons and armor. Indolent toward the Golden Gate, he has no desire to offer his writings or strategies for service.

From time to time, he sings by the riverbank of the "White Moon. This is truly a lofty style. Who can constrain him with floating fame or fleeting profit? Thus he became renowned throughout the monastic community; he was one who lived in total ease and spontaneity.
By means of this, he expresses his emotions and delights in the Way, singing his praises amidst the shadows of water and clouds;
it is truly a game of liberation. Chan Master Chongjuekong of Nan-dang in Lin’an was born in Gushu.

He attended upon Chan Master Sīxīn of Huánglóng, who, regretting that his [Chongjuekong’s] merit did not equal his wisdom, instructed him not to respond to the world. This was written by Master Qing of Cāotáng.
He spoke in verse: "For ten years we gathered at Longfeng Temple; With one awakening to the true void, all phenomena became still.

From now on, following conditions, let us remain in lofty seclusion; Do not let our names fall among the common folk. Thereafter, he sought a dwelling at Mount Tiantai, gazing upon its towering forests.

He was summoned by imperial decree to honor the Buddha’s awakening. Before long, the monastery suffered a fire. Despite his strenuous efforts in the labor of reconstruction, he never grew weary of instructing or receiving visitors.
He once offered this verse on the "Wild Fox" kōan: "To spit blood at others, one first soils one's own mouth; so it was with Baizhang and the wild fox."

He lost his way and ran about wildly; suddenly called back, he performed a somersault. Kongzhi was naturally vigorous and his insight was exceptionally high. He maintained strict discipline over himself and did not attend external invitations.
When someone wished to invite him for a vegetarian feast to construct a triple-gate archway, he replied, "I have already surrendered my household wealth;

it is due to your public devotion that this is being done. To eat food provided by those who turn their backs on the community—how could I, having broken the precepts, endure such a thing? Thus, he remained steadfast in his observance.
It was thus. Yet, in his daily life, his spirit overwhelmed all quarters; even toward his disciples, he seldom showed a favorable countenance.
He truly possessed the character of a father, standing out as one worthy of profound respect.
During the Yuanyou era, Chan Master Touzi Cong and Master Haihui Yan were both renowned for their spiritual stature along the Huai River;

"Not a Buddha, not a thing; his entire body is a single set of golden chain-bones. Zhaozhou went to see the old Nanquan and was able to say, "In Zhenzhou they grow radishes.

"One must recognize that Linji’s little page was none other than the 'white-thief' of those days. Subsequently, Guo Guang went to visit him at Shaowu and also composed a verse in response, saying:
"His entire body is a single set of golden-locked bones; viewed through the true eye, it still remains a superfluous thing."
"Even if one were to point directly to the person before them, I dare say the lay practitioner has not yet reached full penetration.
Miaoxi once remarked that Yuanshao possessed the bearing of a true master, and he also hailed Guang as the "Zen Champion. Surely this is so!
If one follows in the footsteps of the ancients such as Danxia and Pang Jushi, one can truly be said to be beyond reproach.
Chan Master Hongluo of Huqiu had an appearance that seemed quite mild and yielding. He served as the Dharma seat attendant for Chan Master Yuanwu at Daolin Monastery on Mount Tan.
One day, Yuanwu said: "When seeing the seeing, the seeing is not the seeing; even seeing is already apart from seeing."
[Zhaozhou] could not see through it. He then raised his fist and asked, "Do you see? Longtan said, "I see. Yuanwu remarked, "That is like placing a head atop a head.
At these words, Longtan attained realization. Yuanwu subsequently appointed him to oversee the library. Someone asked Yuanwu, "Master Longtan is so gentle and easygoing;
how can he be of any use? Yuanwu replied, "He is a sleeping tiger. Later, when [Longtan] resided at Huqiu, his Way...

This was a great manifestation. Subsequently, while tracing back the story of how Master Baiyun Dan established the Patriarchs’ Hall, he said, "As a descendant, if one cannot personally carry out the bequeathed instructions, is this not contrary to righteousness?
Thereupon, he had portraits painted and enshrined them, composing eulogies above them. Regarding Bodhidharma, he wrote: "The entire nation could not turn him back;

Guleng Guanghui said: "A sudden thunderclap shatters the moon in the clear pool; for three days thereafter, one suffers from deafness.
Once the fatal malady of the *gāohuáng* is removed, the monastic community shall henceforth possess its own tradition.
Kaishan Mingjiao Dashi said: "When spring arrives, the hundred flowers bloom everywhere; their subtle fragrance wafts forth to assail the person. Infinite [beauty] before the wind..."
Profound is its meaning: amidst the clamor of sound and form, not a speck of dust remains. Alas!

Since Baizhang established the monastic regulations of Chan, that the monasteries (*conglin*) have never fallen into ruin is truly rooted in this. Baiyun paired Baizhang’s sacrificial offering with that of Bodhidharma;

among those with discernment, there was none who did not approve of this proposal, for it may be called a recognition of the fundamental source. Since Long was able to follow and uphold these ancestral traditions...

Chan Master Lingyuan resided at the Hall of Silent Illumination (Zhao Mo Tang) in Huanglong; there he engaged in a nocturnal conversation with the layman Donghu, Xu Shichuan.
He then proceeded to relate how Chen Shu once discussed Chan with Dongpo.
Dongpo had remarked that Chen’s talk was like describing the taste of dragon meat, whereas his own discourse was like eating pork—it was truly delicious and genuinely satisfying.
Lingyuan said, "This was something Dongpo said impulsively in his youth; he did not realize he had fallen into error, and I must clarify it for him. Thereupon, they composed two verses.
Verse: Dongpo laughingly spoke of eating dragon meat; who knew that beneath his tongue he had already swallowed its essence?
If one can realize that swallowing its essence is truly flavorful, one will understand that dragon meat is not what is precious. He further said: "How could one know that dragon meat is simply pork?
Subtle words and coarse speech alike enter the divine. Alas, that layman of old failed to shed the root and dust of the great function. Master.
Chuansu laughed and said, "How profound these words! It is a pity that Old Po did not hear them. Alas!
Dongpo’s poem contains the line, 'My former life was surely that of the monk Lu Xingzhe,' which shows he knew for himself that he had come from among the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Yet, when compared to what he learned from Shugushi, it can only be called a previous remark made in jest. Lingyuan wished to block such interpretations and thus composed this commentary.
This is elucidated in verse; how profound its meaning!
Wu Xun of Xingyuan Prefecture, courtesy name Defu, served as the Legal Officer (Facao) of Yuzhang in the first year of the Yuanfeng era.

Thereupon, he took up this question while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, yet for a time he could not trigger the kōan. He then began to read the *Chuan Deng Lu* (The Transmission of the Lamp).

His doubts were never resolved. He then went to Huìtáng to ask him about it. Huìtáng laughed and said, "The way you are currently standing in attendance is 'alignment' (*shùn*)."
"Is this contrary? Wu asked. "It is compliant," he replied. Huìtáng said, "Do you still have doubts? Wu said, "I have no doubts.
Huìtáng said, "Since you yourself have no doubts, why do you doubt that? At these words, Wu attained great enlightenment. He once composed two verses inscribed upon Huìtáng, which read:

"In the midst there are no gates; in the four directions there are no byways. Students labor in vain, busily grasping at shadows. Be careful!"* *Note: This is a traditional Zen expression for taking one's leave.*
The garden moon of a thousand ages: coming tonight as ever, it has never been hidden. Furthermore, an old disciple of Layman Lufeng has captured the Master’s true likeness with perfect intimacy.
Gathering the entire earth to form a single eye, it turns and surges forth in a manner entirely fresh.
Huìtáng composed a verse to see him off: The Haimen Mountains are steep and cut off all traces of footprints; Having trodden the sturdy barrier through, one’s faith is already communicated.
There exists naturally the foundation for a reign of Great Peace; It does not matter whether one is south, north, west, or east. Alas!

Wú served as a subordinate official at the Prefectural Office, yet he was able to set aside his public duties during moments of leisure to resolve his doubts with venerable masters. This is far removed from those who, once they have begun their service as officials, abandon this very matter.
At that time, the monastic communities all admired his character and demeanor; he may truly be called a man of exceptional standing.
Is it not an error for the *Línjiān lù* (Records from the Forest) to refer to Dēfú as Dūnfú?
Chan Master Qian’an Yuan first visited Master Yue of Letan. Yue asked, “Where have you come from? What are you doing here?

If you wish to recognize the pivotal function atop Vulture Peak, it is Mahāprajñāpāramitā. Although he was over eighty years old and had lost his sight, students flocked to him even more closely.
When someone wished to carve his *Yuyao* (Essential Sayings) into woodblocks for circulation, Yuan set himself against it.
He said, "If my words are so deeply in accord with the Buddhas and Patriarchs that my eyesight is restored within one hundred days from now, I shall fulfill your request.
When the period arrived, his sight was indeed healed. Monastics and laypeople praised him with joy, saying, "Is this not a manifestation of Prajñā?
He passed away at the age of ninety-six. In the winter of the Jiyin year of the Jianyan era, less than a few days after his funeral arrangements were completed, the invaders attacked Hongcheng.
In this slaughter, not a single soul was left alive; why did Yuan alone not suffer such calamity? Is it not because he was sustained by the Way and its Virtue?

This caused me to recall Nanquan. At the moment he recalled the word "remember" (憶), [Nanquan] suddenly covered Penglou’s mouth with his hand and said, "Stop! Stop! Penglou was suddenly enlightened.

I only fear that the decline of the Dharma-gate will proceed from this. In the first year of the Zhenghe era, the reign title Chongning was changed to Tianxi.

The *Yi* (Book of Changes) extensively clarifies the light; indeed, affairs originate with companionship (*peng*).

Therefore, I have recorded how [Master] Peng was able to propagate the Sage’s filial piety to the infinite, while simultaneously noting the words of Miaozhan. Miaozhan resided at Xuefeng until his passing.

In the second year of the Yuánfú era, Chan Master Fójian led the assembly of monks at Wǔzǔ. At that time, Tàipíng Língyuán had departed for Huánglóng, leaving the seat vacant.

“Kāśyapa Buddha draped his sixteen-foot golden-banded *kāṣāya* over the body of the thousand-foot Maitreya Buddha;

Discourse: It simply depends on how one practices these principles. First, fortune must not be exhausted; if fortune is exhausted, it will inevitably lead to calamity.
Second, power must not be used to its limit; if power is exhausted, one will certainly suffer humiliation. Third, speech must not be used to its limit.

If one were to speak exhaustively, the opportunity for spiritual resonance would not be secure. Fourth, rules and regulations cannot be applied exhaustively; if they were applied exhaustively, the multitude would find it difficult to abide by them.

Their language is plain while their principles are superior; this is sufficient to remedy faults and keep one far from evil. It is just as medicine does not depend on being refined or coarse; that which cures the illness is what makes it excellent.

It states in brief: "All the True Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Chan gate is revealed herein."
An introduction is provided to recount the circumstances of his encounter, and a verse is offered to reveal the essentials of his school.
When students read this, the essential tenets become clear and the circumstances of the encounter are understood; thus, the general outline of the transmission can be seen.

Now, Qixia was situated between Tiantong and Yuyang, and whenever a monk passed through his gate, he would invariably subject them to examination. One day, there was a monk who claimed to be from Hengyang, and with him—
The Master was from the same village as [the monk]. When the attendant announced his arrival, the Master dragged his staff along, walking and speaking:
"Instead of going away to practice Chan and study the Way, you have come here to recognize a fellow villager. What do you seek? The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him with his staff.

Such was his manner of gathering in beings. The mountain forests surrounding the monastery were deep and beautiful; there, a nobleman had chosen a site for burial, and the funeral procession arrived to meet the coffin.

Fahong lay prostrate in his cave and refused to attend to funeral rites. The Prefect, Imperial Censor Qiu, sent someone to advise him, saying, "The permanent property of a thousand years is for a single day's monk;
why does the Elder suffer by contending over it? Fahong replied, "One must not destroy the permanent property of a thousand years for the sake of a single day's monk.
The nobleman was also a man of virtue; he appreciated these words and changed his course of action. Furthermore, his conduct was of this same character.
Thus it was. Although Hong’s circumstances were not favorable, he took it as his personal responsibility to ensure that the monastery remained for a thousand years;

this alone is sufficient to cause those who cling to their positions out of emotional attachment to feel shame. As for his upright integrity and virtues of diligence and frugality, they were resolute and possessed the majestic spirit of his ancestors;
he may truly be called a grandson of the Great Miao Master Zhe.
In the eighth year of the Shaoxing era, the Giver of Audience Feng Jichuan accompanied the monk Xia to Mount Jing.
He then inscribed a poem on a painting of a withered skull, saying: "The startling form is here; where is the person? Thus one knows that the single spirit does not belong to this skin-bag.
When Master Miaoxi saw it, he said to him, "What kind of understanding is this? Feng immediately composed a verse in response, saying: "Precisely this startling form."
"This is precisely that person; the single spiritual soul within the skin-bag. The skin-bag is the single spiritual soul. Hearing this, Feng was struck with awe and repented, offering his apologies.
At that time, the head seat of the hall, Chan Master Jiuxian Qing, followed suit by saying:

"The physical frame remains here, but where is that person? It is scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind; its luster is obscured, its luster is obscured. Qing was the dharma heir of Master Huirui Yajue.
Chan Master Baofeng Chanti Zhao had five sets of dharma talks that revealed his fundamental teaching principles, which he entrusted to the storekeeper Cong.
The first says: "Caoshan established four prohibitions that encompass the very life-vein of all patch-robed monks. Once you have penetrated them, you must by all means avoid relying upon them.
A person who has accomplished their task must possess a separate path of vital creative energy. The second says: "Patch-robed monks [should seek] within the realm of heterogeneity..."
Regarding conduct: the former masters said that falling into the category of "different species" (icchantika) is the sickness of one who has already understood the matter. Ming’an said:
"One must first recognize the master before it can be attained. Third: the icchantika habitually tells people that they may not practice Chan and may not study the Buddha-dharma.

As long as one is like a great dead person, there is only the fear that upon hearing these words, one will take them to mean "nothingness," or take them to mean "there is no dharma that can satisfy the mind.
This is precisely what it means to be unable to die. If one were truly able to die, one would certainly never entertain such views.
At other times, when among people, you must be especially meticulous. Fourth: My school establishes five ranks as its fundamental principle.

Often, people clarify them through phenomena and principle, harmonize them through quiescence and illumination, perceive them through subject and object, or understand them through essence and function; yet all such approaches fall entirely within the realm of the present moment.
How can it be called the wondrous "special transmission outside the teachings"? At the very head of the path of birth and death, what is the place where one gains strength?
When none of these apply, how can one attempt to calculate or speculate? It will not hit the mark. Fifth: because there is emotion, emotion leaks out.

Because he had vision, there was the outflow of vision; because he had speech, there was the outflow of speech. Even if one were to attain a state devoid of emotion, devoid of vision, and devoid of speech, [Cang] still seized him and asked:
"Who are you? Although an icchantika would not normally grant such a promise lightly, he entrusted [the matter] to Daocong.
This responsibility was truly grave. Daocong must have been one who stood out with exceptional brilliance among the disciples. Indeed!
Why did the World-transcending Master Qingzhi, the Heavenly King, fail to complete his practice before his passing, such that even his name was not heard within the monastic communities?
As for Chan Master Ben of Jianfu Monastery, in the tenth year of the Xiangshu era, he led the assembly of monks at Mount Jing; there, he presented a verse to the Venerable Cong.
Zuo said: "A venomous snake and a fierce tiger stand before one; an iron wall and a silver mountain stretch across behind. There is no door for advancing and no path for retreating.

He presented [the poem] to him. Wu said: "The venomous snake and fierce tiger face each other in vain; the iron wall and silver mountain..."
The mountains are but a delusion; with a single blast of the long flute, it is best to return home. Where else could one seek the "doubting mind"?

Since Wu and I shared the bond of fellow practitioners, we would sing and respond to one another in turn, which was quite different from the casual laughter and drinking that serve as mere diversions for those in office.
Were it not for having attained liberation from all circumstances, how could one have been capable of such things?
The attendant Qing-su of Shi-shuang was born in Mao-yen, Gu-tian, Min. In his later years, he withdrew to Lu-yuan in Xiang-xi, where he cultivated himself through tranquility and simplicity.
At that time, Master Yue of Dou-shui had not yet appeared in the world; he shared a neighboring room with Su.
Once, a guest presented Yue with lychees, and Yue said to Su, "These are the fruits of my native land; we may share them together. Su—
He sighed deeply and said, "Since the passing of my late teacher, I have not seen such a person. Yue followed him and asked, "Who is this master? Su replied, "Ciming.
Yue then took advantage of an opportunity to establish a close connection and inquire further into his teachings.
Yue had previously asked, "Whom have you encountered? Yue told him about Master Zhenjing Wen. Su asked, "And whom did Wen encounter? Yue—
[Qing] Yue said, "Master Nan, Master Su has remarked that since Nan the Junior Monk was at Shishuang not long ago, his Way has flourished to such an extent.

I am increasingly struck by this wonder. He then took incense in his sleeve and sought instruction from him. Su said, "My merit, understanding, and karmic conditions are meager; how could I possibly serve as a teacher for others?"

"However, let me see what your understanding is; try to express it. Yue then set forth his views in detail. Su said, "It is permissible to enter the Buddha-dharma, but one must not enter the realm of Māra.
You must know that the ancients said: 'The final phrase is where one first reaches the secure gate.
As Yue was about to respond, Su suddenly asked again, "How do you explain 'the unconditioned'? Yue was about to respond once more when Su suddenly laughed loudly. Yue was left utterly bewildered.
There was indeed such a person. I once spoke of this to the Layman Wujin (Wujin Jushi), Zhang Gong.
It was in the third year of the Chongning era that the Venerable Jiyin went to Shanxi in Xiazhou to visit Wujin.

Wujin said, "In the past, I met the late Master Zhenjing at Guizong, and we spoke of what is called 'the final phrase' of Doushuai. Before he had even finished speaking, Zhenjing suddenly became enraged."
He scolded him, saying, "This bald-headed fellow who spits blood speaks with deceptive falsehoods; he is not to be trusted.
Seeing his intense anger, [the official] did not dare further explain the details of the matter. Yet, he regretted that Zhenjing did not recognize this. Jiyin said:

"The official knew only the 'final word' transmitted orally by Doushuai, but regarding the True Medicine being present before him, he was unable to perceive it, even though it was the Great Teacher Zhenjing."
Wumen asked, "Why is that? Wujin He said, "Does Zhenjing truly have such an intention? Jiyin replied slowly, "If you doubt, seek it elsewhere.
Under these words, Wujin suddenly saw the scope of Zhenjing’s activity;

he immediately took out the portrait of Zhenjing preserved in his family collection, prostrated before it, and composed a eulogy for it, which he presented to Jiyin, saying: "Yuan'an's fundamental principle is capable of both function and illumination."
With a cold countenance and stern eyes, his divine light shone uniquely. Who could transmit his intent? Only those who beheld him directly could truly emulate him.
First there was Yue, followed by Hong; then Rong and Zhaohu. Later, there was one who engraved a eulogy upon stone at Yangshan.
Jiyin also composed two verses for Yue’s attendant, Zhixuan, which said: "After Master Su passed away, his reputation remains idle; the final word is like the yellow [of the autumn gourd]."
The Stone Inscription: "Having slain all heroes, no one is seen; Zi Lang’s two eyes resemble those of a sorrowful barbarian. It further says:
"How can the two characters 'wuwei' (non-action) be explained? Opening my mouth, I know your illness has grown deeper. I ask the former attendant Xuan:
He neither speaks nor remains silent, yet he smiles with joy. Alas! Yue was able to strike at the essence, yet could not forget its traces. Thus, it led to nothingness.

All who follow fall into this [state]. Were it not for the "Silent Sound" (Muni) dispensing the medicine of true purity to cure the chronic and terminal illness of the inexhaustible, how could such a disease ever be healed?
Truly, the benefits bestowed by the Master upon people are each distinct; how could their ultimate limits ever be easily fathomed?
When Chan Master Foyan Yuan first arrived at Haihui, he relied upon Master Yan.
He consulted him repeatedly regarding his own realization, but Yan would only say to him, "I am not as good as you; you yourself understand it well. Or [Yan] would say, "I do not understand."
"I am not your equal; your meaning is so remote that its limits cannot be fathomed. After a long time, he knocked again and asked, "In this assembly today, who is it that one may draw near?
Yan replied, "There is the Head Seat Yuanli. When you go to him, simply say: 'A patch-robed monk must possess the eye that distinguishes black from white before he can succeed.

Since ancient times, the special envoy has been considered the most important responsibility within a Chan assembly.
One who excels both in ritual propriety and in eloquence fulfills the mission without bringing shame upon it. To remain composed and at ease in this manner—can this not be called a complete talent?

Regarding the fact that many Chan records do not fully preserve the karmic conditions (*nimita*) through which past sages entered the Way, the fault lies with the eminent talents of those times.
The loss of the sequential arrangement was due to a lack of the resolve to protect the school and propagate the Dharma;

consequently, those who see the worthy and desire to emulate them merely end up sighing in deep distress. For a long time, Miaozong has lived in seclusion in a village, hearing nothing of the superior affairs of the monastic centers.
Recently, Ying Zhongwen from Jiangxi traveled from Shuangjing to visit my mountain retreat, and he spoke at length about these former matters.
To hear of his past deeds was a singular consolation for my heart. I then searched through my bag and eventually obtained a volume titled *The Records of Luo Lake*.
What it contained were the refined and beautiful words and deeds of a world-renowned patriarch and virtuous scholar-officials;

there were exchanges of sharp spiritual wit, magnificent prose capable of supporting the religious teachings, and enlightened instructions able to warn future generations. Thereupon, I read them thoroughly and with great care.

I pondered this and could not bear to let go of it. This alone is sufficient to show that Zhongwen’s essentials for the Way and for study are such that his cultivation of the mind far surpasses that of others.

I share this with all those in the world who love the good, hoping that the talented and wise of future generations will follow in his footsteps, causing the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to shine brightly and flourish. Will not his merit in this be vast indeed?
Written respectfully on the twentieth day of the tenth month of the Gengchen year of the Xiangshi era by the Wayfarer Wuzhuo Miaozong of Pilu.
